---
title: "5.1 Bernoulli's Equation"
---

{{< include ../_checkpoint-widget.qmd >}}

## The big idea

For the last two weeks, we saw that, as long as fluids weren't moving,

$$
p = -\rho g z
$$

(where I am going to start using $z$ as the "altitude" coordinate, and going forward we'll need to be careful to have $z$ increasing with altitude). In this reading, we'll derive Bernoulli's equation, which basically adds an extra term to the above equation to factor-in the fluid speed.

Bernoulli's Equation applies to flows with negligible viscosity — a big assumption, but actually it is valid to a lot of our macroscopic world. By ignoring viscous dissipation, we can think from a conservation of energy perspective: Bernoulli's Equation is basically a statement that energy moves between kinetic and potential energies. There are a few nuances — it only applies to a streamline, for example, but it is a very important concept, and "Bernoulli's Principle" is probably something you'll reference throughout your career, even if you forget where the $\rho$ goes in Bernoulli's Equation!

## Think first

**Recall**

1. $\sum F = ma$, and that pressure differences across a body produce a net force.
2. Hydrostatics gave us $p=\rho g h$ when nothing moves.
3. The Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re}_L = \rho U L/\mu$ compares inertia to viscosity.

**Look ahead**

1. What is a *streamline*, and why does Bernoulli's Equation only work along one?
2. If a flow speeds up, does its pressure go up or down?
3. If a duct narrows, why does the flow speed up?

## Streamlines

Bernoulli's Equation applies to fluid parcels along **streamlines**:

> A **streamline** is a line that is everywhere parallel to the velocity vector field.

If you make a quiver (arrow) plot of the velocity field, a streamline is a curve that is always (locally) aligned with those arrows. In steady flow, a streamline is also the path a fluid parcel actually travels. Importantly, this means we can think about that fluid parcel and apply our physics equations to it: conservation of momentum and energy.

::: {.column-margin}
In unsteady flow we also talk about *pathlines* and *streaklines*, which have subtly different meanings (that you can look up, if interested). The one we are focusing on in 3021 is *streamlines*.
:::

Let's think about this picture:

We've sketched a collection of streamlines and highlighted a certain fluid parcel — not a particle traveling with the fluid, a little segment of the fluid itself. This parcel has cross-sectional area $A$ (along the streamline direction). We've got the $\mathbf{\hat{z}}$-direction pointing upwards, against gravity, and have invented two new coordinates: $s$ is our coordinate along a streamline, and $n$ (for normal) is the coordinate perpendicular to that. The length of the fluid parcel we'll call $\Delta s$.

## Newton's second law along a streamline

In this $(s,n)$-coordinate system we can write $\mathbf{F}=m\mathbf{a}$... and let's focus on just the streamline direction:

$$
\sum F_s = m a_s.
$$

- Regarding the forces: we will consider **gravity** and the **forces associated with pressure**...
- ... and we will **neglect viscous forces**, basically assuming $\mu\approx 0$.
- We'll pay attention to just the component of gravity that is acting in the $\hat{s}$-direction. That component is

$$
-mg\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}
$$

::: {.column-margin}
Sanity check: if $z$ is not changing with $s$, $\partial z/\partial s=0$ and we have no component of weight in the streamline direction. This also would mean the streamline is horizontal... makes sense!

If $z$ and $s$ are aligned, we'll have $\partial z/\partial s=1$, and then the component of force in the $\mathbf{\hat{z}}$-direction is $-mg$. Great.
:::

- In the streamline direction, we will say that pressure is acting on the front of the parcel, at position $s+\Delta s$, with area $A$, and on the back of the parcel, at position $s$, with the same area $A$. Invoking a Taylor Series idea, the net force is

$$
\begin{align*}
&-A p(s+\Delta s) + Ap(s)\\
&=-A \left(p(s) + \frac{\partial p}{\partial s}\Delta s\right) + A p(s)\\
&= -A \frac{\partial p}{\partial s}\Delta s.
\end{align*}
$$



- The acceleration term takes a little calculus as well: if the parcel's speed in the streamline direction is $V_s$, then $a_s = \partial V_s/\partial t$. But we also recognize that $V_s$ is a function of $s$: $V_s(s(t))$. Then we can apply the chain rule:

$$
\frac{\partial V_s}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial s}{\partial t}\frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s} = V_s \frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s}.
$$

::: {.column-margin}
The last step is: $\frac{\partial s}{\partial t}=V_s$, the change in streamline position with time is the same as the streamline velocity.
:::

Combining these together, the conservation of momentum becomes

$$
-mg\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}-A \frac{\partial p}{\partial s}\Delta s = m V_s \frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s}.
$$

A couple more observations:

- $A\Delta s$ is the volume of the fluid parcel.
- $m$ is the density times volume.

That means each of these terms includes volume. Let's bring all the terms onto the same side of the equation, and then divide through by volume to get 

$$
 0=\frac{\partial p}{\partial s}+ \rho V_s \frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s} +\rho g\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}.
$$

Now: integrate this whole equation with respect to $s$. The first and last terms are easy, e.g.

$$
 \int \frac{\partial p}{\partial s} ds = \int dp = p +\text{ constant}.
$$

The middle term is a little bit trickier, but I'll tell you the result and you can check it easily (easier to differentiate than integrate):

$$
\int \rho V_s \frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s} ds = \frac12 \rho V_s^2 +\text{ constant}. 
$$

::: {.column-margin}
The check:

$$
\begin{align*}
&\frac{\partial}{\partial s}\left( \frac12 \rho V_s^2\right)\\
&= \frac12 \rho \left( 2 V_s \frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s}\right)\\
&= \rho V_s \frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s}
\end{align*}
$$

good.
:::

After completing the integration...

::: {.callout-important}
## Bernoulli's Equation

$$
p + \frac{1}{2}\rho V^2 + \rho g z = \text{constant along a streamline}.
$$

(We dropped the subscript $s$, and all of the constants of integration can be combined into a single constant.)
:::

This is one equation mechanical engineers actually memorize, or at least the principle behind it. The "Bernoulli Principle" is that an increase in flow speed **decreases** the pressure. This principle is used to explain phenomena like:

- **Airfoil lift.** Faster flow over the top of a wing means less pressure on top of the wing. Hence, a lift force.
- **Entrainment.** Moving air is lower pressure so it "sucks in" extra air.


## How do we use Bernoulli's Equation?

The basic case: suppose two positions, "1" and "2", are connected by a streamline. The quantity $p + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 + \rho g z$ is constant along a streamline, which means

$$
p_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho V_1^2 + \rho g z_1 =
p_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho V^2_2 + \rho g z_2.
$$

Often, we will know everything about position 1, and some information about position 2. That is, $p_1$, $V_1$, and $z_1$ might be known, along with the altitude and speed at position two: $z_2$ and $V_2$. Then

$$
p_2 = p_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho (V_1^2-V_2^2) + \rho g (z_1-z_2).
$$

::: {.column-margin}
See below a brief introduction to conservation of mass — this is how we might determine the speed $V_2$.
:::

## What does it mean?

Step back: we were looking at conservation of momentum, $F_s = m a_s$, and then we integrated with respect to $s$, a distance coordinate. (We also divided by volume, but that is not important.) What is force times distance? **Work.** And work is related to **energy**: Bernoulli's Equation is basically a statement of conservation of energy.

::: {.column-margin}
Tempting, especially after last week, to say force times distance is a moment! In this case we aren't talking lever arms though.
:::

Look at the terms:

- $\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2$. That is a kinetic energy per volume.
- $\rho g z$. That is a gravitational potential energy per volume.
- $p$. A little bit trickier to interpret... it's actually related to the amount of flow work, if you've taken thermodynamics. I like to interpret it as: we can use work to increase the pressure of a fluid, and then that elevated pressure is a kind of potential energy.

Importantly, by neglecting viscosity, there are no **energy dissipation terms**: the total amount of (mechanical) energy present in the flow at position 1 is the same as the total amount of energy present in the flow at position 2.

## When can we use Bernoulli's Equation?

One of the most important lessons we learn in fluid mechanics is **when can we make simplifying assumptions**. Bernoulli's Equation is so nice! It is just algebra! 

We'll see the [Navier-Stokes Equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navier–Stokes_equations) soon... they are nonlinear partial differential equations in three dimensions and are ostensibly a complete representation of flow physics (for Newtonian fluids). They are also practically unsolvable.

Bernoulli's Equation is easy to "solve", but is only applicable in specific scenarios. Namely: we assumed negligible viscosity. We can frame this in terms of the Reynolds Number:

$$
\mathrm{Re}_L = \frac{\rho U L}{\mu},
$$

and then say: Bernoulli's Equation is applicable when $\mathrm{Re} \gg 1$. (In such a case, the fluid inertia is much much larger than the fluid dissipation.)

There are a few caveats which we might not understand for a few more weeks. These are related to certain "high Reynolds Number phenomena" that actually require viscosity to occur.

- **Boundary layers** form near surfaces during high-Re flows — very thin layers over which the fluid transitions from high speed to zero velocity to meet the no-slip condition. Bernoulli's Equation does not work within the boundary layers, but is still often applied outside the boundary layers.
- **Vortices** occur in moderate-to-high-Re flows, particularly in the wake of blunt bodies like spheres and cylinders. Viscosity is necessary to describe their formation, and additionally their existence complicates the "along a streamline" description.
- **Turbulence** occurs at high Reynolds Numbers. Viscosity is again relevant, and again the streamline description is difficult to apply.

Despite this: if you (an object that is more-or-less 1 m large) are walking on a day with a slight breeze (5 m/s), the Reynolds Number is something like 300000... definitely much much larger than one. This is to say: a lot of everyday life occurs at a Reynolds Number where Bernoulli's Equation is applicable.






## Quick additional thing: a basic statement of conservation of mass

To actually *use* Bernoulli we almost always need a second equation — we might know our second location, $z_2$, but won't necessarily know the pressure, $p_2$, or speed, $V_2$, there. Bernoulli's Equation is then one equation, two unknowns — we need some more information.

Consider a duct that narrows: uniform flow enters at speed $U_1$ and pressure $p_1$ through area $A_1$, and leaves through a smaller area $A_2$. What is the speed at $A_2$?

```{=html}
  <path d="M 70 70 L 320 70 C 355 70 355 120 390 120 L 560 120

  <line x1="120" y1="75" x2="120" y2="200" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4,3"/>
  <line x1="120" y1="95"  x2="175" y2="95"  stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#duct-arrow-blue)"/>
  <line x1="120" y1="122" x2="175" y2="122" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#duct-arrow-blue)"/>
  <line x1="120" y1="150" x2="175" y2="150" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#duct-arrow-blue)"/>
  <line x1="120" y1="178" x2="175" y2="178" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#duct-arrow-blue)"/>
  <text x="18" y="100" font-size="14" fill="#2b6ca3">uniform</text>
  <text x="30" y="128" font-size="16" fill="#2b6ca3"><tspan font-style="italic">U</tspan><tspan font-size="11" dy="4">1</tspan></text>
  <text x="30" y="160" font-size="16" fill="#8e44ad"><tspan font-style="italic">p</tspan><tspan font-size="11" dy="4">1</tspan></text>

  <!-- area labels -->
  <line x1="245" y1="240" x2="245" y2="210" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#duct-arrow)"/>
  <text x="252" y="248" font-size="16" fill="#c0392b"><tspan font-style="italic">A</tspan><tspan font-size="11" dy="4">1</tspan></text>
  <line x1="245" y1="35" x2="245" y2="64" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#duct-arrow)"/>

  <line x1="470" y1="215" x2="470" y2="181" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#duct-arrow)"/>
  <text x="477" y="223" font-size="16" fill="#c0392b"><tspan font-style="italic">A</tspan><tspan font-size="11" dy="4">2</tspan></text>
  <line x1="470" y1="85" x2="470" y2="114" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#duct-arrow)"/>
</svg>
</div>
```

For a cross-section over which the velocity is constant, the **mass flow rate** is

$$
\dot{m} = \rho U A, \qquad \left[\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{s}}\right] = \left[\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^3}\right]\left[\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}\right]\left[\text{m}^2\right].
$$

::: {.column-margin}
We sometimes work with the **volumetric flow rate** instead, particularly when dealing with constant density systems. For some reason we use the symbol $Q$, and $Q=\dot{m}/\rho$, in m³/s.
:::

Conservation of mass for this duct says whatever goes in must come out:

$$
\dot{m}_1 = \dot{m}_2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \rho U_1 A_1 = \rho U_2 A_2 \quad (\rho = \text{const})
$$

and so we can say 
$$
\Rightarrow\quad U_2 = U_1 \frac{A_1}{A_2}.
$$

This is a brief statement of **conservation of mass**, applicable when the flow at position 1 is a constant speed, and the flow at position 2 is a constant (possibly different) speed. We'll see later how to modify this for more complicated flows, but this will be a nice tool to have when we are first solving problems with Bernoulli's Equation.

## Earn it — 2 quick gates

We now have both equations we need, so let's check that we can reason with them *before* reaching for algebra. A steady flow passes through a tube that narrows, so $A_1 > A_2$.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="What happens to the speed? Type 1 if it increases, −1 if it decreases."
     data-answer="1" data-tol="0.05" data-units=""
     data-hint="The same mass has to get through a smaller opening every second. Does it have to hurry or dawdle?"
     data-solution="It increases. Conservation of mass gives U₂ = U₁·A₁/A₂, and A₁/A₂ > 1, so U₂ > U₁."
     data-target="bern-gate-speed"
     data-ok-text="&#10003; yes — a narrower tube means a faster flow."></div>
```

::: {#bern-gate-speed .fl-hidden}
It speeds up. Same mass per second, smaller cross-section, so it has to increase in speed.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="What happens to its pressure? Type 1 if it increases, −1 if it decreases."
     data-answer="-1" data-tol="0.05" data-units=""
     data-hint="Bernoulli's constant is fixed along the streamline. You just decided the ½ρV² term goes up — so something else has to come down."
     data-solution="It decreases. p + ½ρV² + ρgz is constant along the streamline and z doesn't change, so if ½ρV² goes up, p must go down."
     data-target="bern-gate-pressure"
     data-ok-text="&#10003; correct — faster flow, lower pressure."></div>
```
:::

::: {#bern-gate-pressure .fl-hidden}
The pressure *drops*. This might be non-intuitive: squeezing flow through a tube should raise the pressure inside it, the way squeezing a balloon does. But the fluid isn't being squeezed — it's being *accelerated*, and the thing pushing the flow to make it accelerate is pressure (a higher pressure upstream than downstream).
:::
